reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A common, chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins presenting with burning, grittiness, crusting, and redness that is typically bilateral and worse in the mornings
Divided into anterior blepharitis (affecting the lash bases, often staphylococcal or seborrhoeic) and posterior blepharitis (meibomian gland dysfunction)
Anterior staphylococcal disease shows hard crusts and collarettes around the lashes, with lash loss and misdirection in chronic cases
Posterior disease shows capped, plugged, or inspissated meibomian orifices and a poor-quality, foamy tear film with associated evaporative dry eye
Strongly associated with rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis; recurrent chalazia and styes are common complications
The mainstay of management is lid hygiene with warm compresses and lid margin cleaning; topical antibiotic ointment helps anterior disease and oral tetracyclines help refractory meibomian dysfunction
Recurrent, unilateral, or asymmetrical lid margin disease with lash loss should raise suspicion of eyelid malignancy such as sebaceous gland carcinoma
Patients should be counselled that it is a chronic, relapsing condition controlled rather than cured
reference.pathophysiology: Blepharitis is chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins with overlapping mechanisms. Anterior blepharitis involves bacterial (chiefly staphylococcal) colonisation of the lash bases and an inflammatory reaction to bacterial products, or seborrhoeic changes with excessive scaling. Posterior blepharitis reflects meibomian gland dysfunction, in which altered and inspissated meibomian secretions block the glands, destabilise the lipid layer of the tear film, and promote evaporative dry eye. Bacterial lipases and inflammatory mediators contribute to ocular surface irritation, and the condition is frequently linked to rosacea.
additionalDifferentials: Sebaceous gland carcinoma of the eyelid (in atypical, unilateral disease)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination of the lid margins, lashes, and meibomian gland orifices
Assessment of tear film stability and ocular surface staining for associated dry eye
Lid margin or lash swab in severe or atypical cases
Lid margin biopsy when malignancy is suspected (unilateral disease with lash loss and induration)
redFlags: Unilateral or markedly asymmetrical disease with localised lash loss and lid thickening suggesting sebaceous gland carcinoma
Associated corneal involvement (marginal keratitis or ulceration) threatening vision
Failure to respond to appropriate treatment prompting re-evaluation of the diagnosis
Recurrent chalazia at the same site raising concern for malignancy
reference.prognosis: Blepharitis is a chronic relapsing condition that is generally controlled well with sustained lid hygiene, though symptoms recur if treatment lapses; complications such as recurrent chalazia and evaporative dry eye can be troublesome but vision is usually preserved.
pitfalls: Expecting a cure rather than long-term control and stopping lid hygiene prematurely
Missing sebaceous gland carcinoma masquerading as recurrent unilateral blepharitis or chalazion
Overlooking associated dry eye and rosacea that require concurrent management
Prolonged unmonitored topical steroid use with risk of raised intraocular pressure
management: Lid hygiene as the mainstay — warm compresses and lid-margin cleaning sustained over the long term
Topical antibiotic ointment for anterior staphylococcal disease
Oral tetracyclines for refractory posterior blepharitis and meibomian gland dysfunction
Ocular lubricants to manage the associated evaporative dry eye
Treat coexistent rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis
Manage complications such as recurrent chalazia and styes
Consider lid-margin biopsy for unilateral disease with lash loss and induration to exclude malignancy
